A runaway is something or someone that has broken free from control and is now moving, acting, or existing outside the bounds of where it should be — often in a way that is hard or impossible to stop.
The Most Common Use: A Person

The most frequent meaning of runaway as a noun is a person — almost always a child or teenager — who has secretly left home without permission and without telling anyone where they are going.

This person hasn't just gone for a walk. They've made a deliberate choice to leave, usually because something at home has become unbearable — abuse, conflict, extreme unhappiness, or fear. They are now living on their own, without their family's knowledge or approval.

"The police found the runaway hiding in an abandoned building."

"The shelter downtown takes in runaways and helps connect them with social workers."

Notice that the word itself carries a quiet weight. When you hear "a runaway," you instinctively sense vulnerability and urgency. It is not a neutral word. It suggests someone in trouble, someone escaping from something painful, and often someone who is now in danger.

Historically, the word was also used for enslaved people who escaped to freedom — people who literally ran away from captivity. This older usage still lives in historical writing.
A Runaway Can Also Be an Animal

The second common use of runaway as a noun refers to an animal — typically a horse — that has broken free from its handler and is running out of control.

"The runaway galloped straight through the marketplace before anyone could stop it."

A horse is powerful. When one breaks loose and bolts, no one can simply grab it and make it stop. That sense of uncontrollable momentum is exactly what the word captures.
A Runaway Can Also Be a Vehicle

A runaway can also refer to a vehicle — a truck, a train, a cart — that is moving without anyone controlling it, usually because the brakes have failed or no one is at the wheel.

"Emergency crews worked to slow the runaway before it reached the crowded station."

This is the same underlying idea: something that was supposed to be under control has broken free and is now going wherever momentum takes it.
What All These Meanings Have in Common

No matter whether the runaway is a teenager, a horse, or a truck — the word always signals three things:

  1. Escape — it has left where it was supposed to be.
  2. Loss of control — no one is currently steering or stopping it.
  3. Urgency — the situation demands immediate attention.

This is what makes runaway such a vivid word. It doesn't just describe movement. It describes movement that has gone rogue.

As a noun, it follows normal rules:

  • One person: a runaway
  • Many people: runaways

"The city's shelters were overwhelmed by the number of runaways seeking help."

There is a difference between someone who runs away (the action) and someone who is a runaway (the identity or label).

  • "She ran away from home last Thursday." → This describes what she did.
  • "She is a runaway." → This describes who she now is — someone living outside the home, unaccounted for.

The noun runaway is the label given to someone once running away has become their situation, not just a momentary act.

A runaway (noun) is a person (especially a young person who has fled home), an animal, or a vehicle that has escaped from control and is now moving or existing in an uncontrolled, unsanctioned way — often urgently and dangerously. The word always carries the idea of something that broke free and cannot easily be brought back.
